description: Batuk Bhairav is worshipped in Varanasi as the child form of Kaal Bhairav, himself a fierce manifestation of Shiva and traditionally regarded as a guardian of Kashi. A local temple listing places the shrine in the Kamachha area, and describes the deity as the one who, as a child, is said to have protected the city and slain the demon Andhakasur. The Kashi Khand, as summarised by a Varanasi temples site, describes eight Bhairavs stationed around Kashi to shield devotees; Batuk Bhairav is a separate, widely visited Bhairav shrine in the city, reported to lie close to the Krodhan (Adi) Bhairav temple. Visitor guides describe an Akhand Deep, a lamp said to have burned continuously for ages, whose oil devotees believe has healing properties; the temple is also associated with Aghori and Tantric worship. Typical offerings mentioned are coconut, black sesame seeds, red flowers and mustard oil, and a dog is honoured on the premises as the deity's attendant. Devotees perform mantra recitation, havan and lamp offerings here, with morning and evening aarti.

description: Chamundeshwari Temple stands on Chamundi Hills, roughly 13 km from Mysuru in Karnataka. It is dedicated to Chamundeshwari, identified with Durga and worshipped as Mahishasura Mardini, the slayer of the buffalo demon; she is regarded as the tutelary deity of the Wodeyar royal family. According to Wikipedia, the original shrine is thought to date to the 12th century and was likely built by Hoysala rulers, while the tower is probably a 17th-century Vijayanagar-era addition. A flight of about 1,000 steps up the hill was built in 1659, and a large granite Nandi sits along the climb. Navaratri is the temple's main festival and is closely tied to the Mysuru Dasara celebrations, when the goddess is decorated in different forms. Local tradition holds that the site is a Shakti Peetha, said to be where Sati's hair fell; this is a traditional attribution rather than a verified fact.

description: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha stands on the bank of Ulsoor (Halasuru) Lake in Bengaluru, roughly 7 km from the Majestic area, with Halasuru the nearest metro station according to Karnataka Tourism. A 2004 Deccan Herald feature, reproduced on a blog, reports that the building was constructed in 1943, inaugurated in 1945 and extended with a first floor in 1975, with the Jolly and Sahni families and wider community donations credited for its construction. Both that article and Karnataka Tourism describe it as the largest Sikh shrine in the city. Karnataka Tourism notes a large prayer hall housing the Guru's seat and a marble palanquin, Guru ka Langar (community meal) served on Sundays, and a convention hall and school run by the management. The gurdwara serves Bengaluru's Sikh community.

description: The Thiyaganur Buddha statues, also known as the Perambalur Buddhas, are a group of seated Buddha images in villages of Tamil Nadu. According to Wikipedia, the main site is Thiyaganur, a village in Salem district's Thalaivasal taluk, where two images about 1.8 m (6 ft) tall are found. One is enshrined in a small pillared compound; the other, on a private farm, was later housed in a Buddhist meditation hall (Dhyana Mandap) built in 2013 with public contributions. Further images are in nearby villages such as Paravai and Okalur, the latter locally nicknamed 'Dubai Buddha'. Historians date the images to about the 11th century, and Tamil Nadu Tourism lists them among the state's Buddhist sites. Villagers worship the figures in a local devotional style, calling the deity 'Buddha Samy'. Wikipedia notes that some images are in poor condition and that experts identify one at Perumathur as a Jain Tirthankara.

description: Kukke Subramanya Temple is a Hindu temple on the banks of the Kumaradhara river at Subramanya, in Sullia taluk of Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka. It is dedicated to Subrahmanya (Kartikeya), worshipped here in close association with serpent deities. According to local tradition, the serpent king Vasuki sought refuge here from Garuda, and Wikipedia notes that the temple is counted among seven sites said to have been established by Parashurama. One temple guide describes a silver-covered Garuda pillar before the sanctum, which enshrines Subrahmanya, Vasuki and Shesha. Sarpa Samskara, a rite performed for relief from serpent-related afflictions, is associated with the temple, and festivals include Shasti, Kiru Shasti and Nagara Panchami. Wikipedia records that the temple is now administered by the Karnataka Endowment Department, and that its priesthood passed to Shivalli Brahmins after 1845.
